title: Ki Teitzei: pay today (Deuteronomy 24:14–15)
hook: don't hold a poor worker's wages overnight

segments.voice: Yesterday, the railing around the roof, built before anyone falls. Your line was build the railing. Did you fix your hazard? Today, a law about the end of a work day. Day five hundred nine.

For a lot of people, payday decides what's for dinner. A delivery driver waiting on a platform to release last week's earnings. A freelancer chasing an invoice that's sixty days late. A day laborer outside a hardware store at six in the morning, hoping the cash comes at the end of the shift and not next Friday. For the person paying, a delay is a line on a to-do list. For the person waiting, it's groceries, or not. The Torah draws the line at sunset.
screen: `PAYDAY DECIDES DINNER.` → `AN INVOICE SIXTY DAYS LATE.` → `THE LINE AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: First, the Torah says, don't oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether they're one of your own people or a stranger living in your towns. Then the rule, in the old Jewish translation: "In the same day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it." Leviticus says it too, from the other side of the clock: don't keep a worker's wages with you overnight until morning. The rabbis called this prohibition bal talin, do not hold it overnight. Now look at the reason. For he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it. In Hebrew, the phrase is closer to: he lifts up his soul to it. His whole self is hanging on that pay. The Talmud, in Bava Metzia, reads those words and asks: why did this worker climb the high ramp, hang from the tree, risk his life? For his wages. So when you hold back what he earned, the Talmud says, it's as if you've taken his life. That's strong language for a late payment. But it's the worker's view, not the employer's. The one who pays sees an amount. The one who's paid sees a day of his life, already spent, waiting to come back as bread. The verse ends with a warning: or he will cry to the LORD against you, and it will be counted as sin. The cry of the unpaid is heard.
screen: `DON'T OPPRESS THE POOR WORKER.` · `BEFORE THE SUN GOES DOWN.` · `HE LIFTS UP HIS SOUL TO IT.` · `HE CLIMBED, HUNG, RISKED HIS LIFE.` · then, large: `PAY TODAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay one bill or debt promptly. Settle, and breathe. Think of what you owe that's sitting on your list. Not just bills. The babysitter you meant to pay back. The friend who covered lunch. The contractor's invoice. The kid down the street who mowed the lawn. Picture the person on the other end, not the amount. What are they waiting to do with it? Choose one, and decide to pay it before today's sunset. The bell holds the time.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. The portion where a worker's pay can't wait past sundown.
Your line: pay today. Before the sun goes down, pay one person you owe, especially someone who works for you. Day five hundred nine.

screen: `DAY 509 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KI TEITZEI: THE FORGOTTEN SHEAF (DEUTERONOMY 24:19).`

howItsDone: Jewish law forbids delaying payment to workers past the agreed time, called bal talin, and observant employers, from families paying a babysitter to businesses, are taught to pay day workers by the end of the day or night they worked.
